Weather · The Big Story

The storm is violent. The forecast is not a Japan landfall.

Typhoon Koguma carried gusts of 65 meters per second east of Japan this morning. The same official forecast turns it north over open water. Understanding both facts is the difference between useful caution and panic.

What to do now

As of the Japan Meteorological Agency’s 7:05 a.m. update on October 11, the forecast did not show Koguma making landfall on Japan’s main islands. People in and around the Ogasawara Islands and anyone planning coastal or marine activity should still check current JMA warnings and wave information; forecasts change.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 11, 2026 · 08:15 JST · 9 min read

At 6 a.m. Japan time, a tight spiral of rain bands was turning over the Pacific near 24.1° north, 148.5° east. That point is far east of the Japanese archipelago, roughly in the ocean southeast of the Ogasawara chain. At its center, Typhoon No. 29—Koguma—had a pressure of 950 hectopascals. The Japan Meteorological Agency classified it as a “very strong typhoon.”

The numbers are severe. Maximum sustained winds near the center were 45 meters per second, about 162 kilometers per hour. Gusts could reach 65 m/s, or 234 km/h. Storm-force winds extended 130 kilometers from the center, while gale-force winds reached 330 kilometers to the north and 280 kilometers to the south. The JAXA observation above shows why those numbers cannot be dismissed: the storm has a compact, organized core surrounded by curved bands of heavy precipitation.

But intensity and destination are different questions. A powerful storm can remain offshore; a weaker one can still produce damaging rain or waves if its path brings hazards to land. The JMA’s 7:05 a.m. update projected Koguma moving northwest at 20 km/h, then bending north and northeast. Its forecast centers remained over the Pacific east of Japan.

The surprise is not that Koguma is weak. It is that a genuinely violent cyclone can be both meteorologically serious and, on the current track, not a forecast landfall for Japan.

The track in five official checkpoints

Oct 12 · 06:0027.7N, 147.3E
955 hPa · 45 m/s
Oct 13 · 03:0032.4N, 149.5E
970 hPa · 40 m/s
Oct 14 · 03:0038.4N, 156.6E
980 hPa · 30 m/s
Oct 15 · 03:0043.1N, 165.1E
Extratropical low

The forecast does not draw a train track. Each later point comes with a probability circle: the center is expected to fall somewhere inside that circle 70 percent of the time. At 6 p.m. Sunday, the circle’s radius was 55 kilometers. By early Thursday, the radius widened to 320 kilometers. Uncertainty grows with time, which is why a four-day map should never be read as an exact itinerary.

JMA expected Koguma to remain “very strong” through Monday morning, then weaken to a typhoon by early Tuesday and a severe tropical storm by Wednesday. By early Thursday it was forecast to become an extratropical low well northeast of Japan. That transition does not mean hazardous weather instantly disappears. JMA explicitly warns that heavy rain, strong winds and high waves can continue after a cyclone changes category.

This is the first small discovery hidden inside the forecast language: “extratropical” describes a storm’s structure and energy source, not a harmlessness switch. A former typhoon can expand, accelerate and affect a broad area even while its tropical core weakens.

Why an offshore storm still belongs in a Japan brief

Japan includes remote Pacific islands that disappear on many world maps. Minamitorishima, Japan’s easternmost territory, lies about 1,850 kilometers southeast of Tokyo. The Ogasawara Islands stretch south into the same oceanic space through which western North Pacific cyclones frequently turn. “East of Japan” is not the same as “irrelevant to Japan,” especially for ships, fishing operations, island transport and exposed coastlines.

Long-period swell can travel far from a cyclone’s center. It may arrive under blue sky, producing surf that looks less threatening than the storm that generated it. That is why the responsible message is not “Japan is safe” or “Japan is being hit.” It is narrower: no main-island landfall appears on this morning’s official track, but people making marine decisions should use the newest local warnings, not this article’s cutoff.

A second discovery sits in the storm’s name. Koguma is the Japanese contribution to the regional naming list and means the constellation Ursa Minor—the Little Bear. Names in the western North Pacific are contributed by members of the World Meteorological Organization’s Typhoon Committee and used in sequence. The gentle name does not describe intensity.

The storm also has another identifier, 27W, used by the U.S. Joint Typhoon Warning Center. Those systems count differently. Japan’s “Typhoon No. 29” refers to the 29th tropical cyclone of the year to reach typhoon strength under JMA’s regional system, while 27W is a separate basin identifier. Two numbers do not mean two storms.

The other cyclone on the map

Koguma was not alone. JMA also tracked Typhoon No. 28, Nolo, east of Japan. Nolo’s backstory is unusual: it formed in the eastern Pacific as a hurricane and crossed the International Date Line, where the regional label changed from hurricane to typhoon. The circulation did not vanish at midnight on an imaginary line; the vocabulary changed because responsibility moved between meteorological basins.

By early October 11, Nolo was much weaker than Koguma, with a central pressure near 996 hPa and maximum winds around 20 m/s. Its broad gale area nevertheless extended hundreds of kilometers. Seeing two numbered systems east of Japan makes a dramatic map, but the systems must be assessed separately. Koguma’s compact core, Nolo’s weaker circulation, their distances from land and their projected paths all matter more than the count.

The broader 2026 season supplies another striking number. Weathernews reported that 2026 joined 1965 and 2015 as only the third year in JMA’s record since 1951 with a typhoon forming in every month from January through October. That statistic describes an unusual calendar distribution, not proof by itself of a trend or the cause of any individual storm. Climate conclusions require longer records and attribution research.

How to read 950 hPa without being misled

Central pressure is one measure of cyclone intensity, but it is not a direct damage forecast. A lower pressure generally accompanies stronger circulation, yet impacts depend on size, track, forward speed, terrain, tides and the distribution of rain. Koguma’s 950 hPa center and 45 m/s winds justify its “very strong” category; they do not tell a Tokyo resident that 45 m/s winds are coming to Tokyo.

The unit conversion matters too. JMA’s 45 m/s is a ten-minute sustained wind. Other agencies may use one-minute averages, producing a different-looking number for the same storm. Comparisons across agencies should identify the averaging period before declaring that one estimate is “stronger.”

Readers should also distinguish the forecast center from the storm-warning area. The probability circle shows where the center may be. The warning-area envelope accounts for the storm’s wind field around those possible centers. A coastline can experience swell or strong wind without the center crossing it.

What changes the story next

Three things deserve attention after today’s edition. First, does the forecast bend farther west or east as Koguma turns north? Second, how quickly does the core weaken after Monday? Third, do local meteorological offices issue wave or wind warnings for the Ogasawara Islands or Pacific coasts? Those are concrete signals; viral screenshots without an issue time are not.

Use JMA’s live tropical-cyclone page for the track, then open the warning and high-wave pages for the place that matters to you. The official map’s timestamp is as important as its colored lines. If a warning conflicts with this article, follow the newer warning.

Today’s Japanese word is 進路 (shinro), “course” or “path.” 進 means advance; 路 means road or route. In daily life it can describe a student’s future course after school. In weather news, taifū no shinro means a typhoon’s projected path. The useful habit is to pair the word with yohō, forecast: a predicted shinro is not a fixed road.
